newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Explosives attached to remote control -- UN.
newsitem.headline: Explosives attached to remote control -- UN.

text.p: A U.N. spokesman said on Saturday that mines found under a bridge in Sarajevo hours before the scheduled arrival of Pope John Paul II were connected to a detonator and a remote control device.
"It seems a worker saw a person in that area this morning and advised the police," Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the United Nations mission, told Reuters.
"On arrival the Bosnian police and the International Police Task Force found 23 mines connected to a detonator with additional plastic explosives and a remote control," Ivanko said.
Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation bomb experts believed the explosives were "freshly planted", he added.
Bosnian authorities and international police officers met to discuss the security situation ahead of the arrival of the Pope at Sarajevo airport later on Saturday.
Earlier, a Bosnian police officer said more than 20 mines were found under the bridge on the main boulevard Mesa Selimovic.
"We inspected the bridge yesterday and there was nothing there," the polceman said.
Sarajevo authorities declined to comment on whether the Pope's motorcade planned to pass along the road, but visiting dignitaries usually use the boulevard to and from the airport.
Large numbers of policemen have been posted along the boulevard which leads to the city centre.
A series of bomb attacks on Roman Catholic churches and Islamic mosques in the past two months had raised concerns for the Pope's safety during his historic two-day visit.
Bosnian police, supported by the NATO-led peace force, announced elaborate security precautions this week, deploying bomb disposal and anti-sniper teams.
The Pope was forced to cancel a scheduled visit in September 1994 while the war was still raging. Bosnian Serb forces laying siege to the city refused to give security guarantees.
The Serb member of the new collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, supported the invitation for this week's Papal trip.
